title: The hare and the lynx
teaches: Why predators and prey rise and fall in cycles, and why fishing both can help the prey

blocks.text: For over two hundred years the Hudson's Bay Company bought furs from trappers across northern Canada, and it kept careful books. Every year its posts recorded how many pelts of each animal came in: beaver, marten, fox, muskrat, and the Canada lynx, a big-footed wild cat of the northern forest. In the 1920s the Oxford ecologist Charles Elton went through the Company's records and noticed that the lynx numbers rose and fell in a regular ten-year rhythm.[^elton] At a peak, trappers brought in tens of thousands of lynx; in a trough a few years later, they could hardly find any.

Lynx eat snowshoe hares, and little else in winter. When Elton and others put the hare records beside the lynx, the hares followed the same rhythm, and the lynx peaks came a year or two after the hares'. The hare cycle was well known to the people of the north. In a peak year hares were everywhere, stripping the bark from willows; in a crash year a hunter could walk all day and not see one.

blocks.text: Why should two populations swing up and down, again and again, with the predator always a little behind? Lesson 2's yeast rose and stopped; lesson 3's reindeer rose and crashed once. The hares and lynx do something different: they never settle.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Hudson's Bay Company fur records show lynx and snowshoe hares cycling roughly every ten years.
Lynx peaks come a year or two after hare peaks.

blocks.text: In 1925 the American physical chemist Alfred Lotka, and in 1926, independently, the Italian mathematician Vito Volterra, wrote down the simplest model of a predator and its prey. Each population is a stock, as in lesson 2, and each one's flows depend on the other.

Hares are born in proportion to how many hares there are, as Darwin's elephants were. They die mostly by being eaten, and the number eaten depends on how often a lynx meets a hare, which goes up with both the number of hares and the number of lynx. Lynx are born in proportion to the hares they eat, since a well-fed lynx raises kittens and a starving one doesn't. They die at a steady rate when there's nothing to eat. Two stocks, four flows.

blocks.caption: Lotka and Volterra's model of hares and lynx, in thousands. Left: both over time. Right: the same run as a loop, hares across and lynx up.
blocks.task: Guess, then play at least twenty years

blocks.text: With few lynx, hares multiply. With many hares, lynx eat well and multiply, but they can only multiply as fast as the hares feed them, so their numbers trail behind. When lynx are many, hares are eaten faster than they breed, and their numbers fall. The lynx keep rising for a while, living on the hares that are left, then starve and fall. With few lynx, the hares recover, and the whole thing starts again. Hare peaks come first and lynx peaks after, as in the Company's books.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: In Lotka and Volterra's model, prey are born in proportion to prey and eaten in proportion to meetings with predators; predators are born from prey eaten and die when there's nothing to eat.
Two stocks whose flows depend on each other can cycle: prey up, predators up, prey down, predators down.

blocks.text: The right-hand graph in the figure shows the same run in a different way. Instead of time along the bottom, it puts hares across and lynx up, so that each moment is a single point. As time passes the point moves, and in Lotka and Volterra's model it goes round and round the same closed loop forever, anticlockwise. Ecologists call this a **phase plot**, and it's a quick way to see whether a system cycles, settles or runs away.

In the pure model the size of the loop depends only on where it starts. That is a fragile property: any small change to the model alters it. Switch on the hares' food limit, so that hares are held back by their own crowding as well as by lynx, and the loop spirals inward. The two populations settle down to steady numbers. The Lotka-Volterra cycles show that predator and prey can swing, though they do not fully explain why the real hares and lynx keep doing so.

Real ledgers are not so tidy either. Show the Company's numbers on the figure and you'll see peaks of different heights and gaps of eight to eleven years. In 1973 the ecologist Michael Gilpin plotted the fur returns as a loop and found that in some decades it ran backwards, as if the hares were eating the lynx.[^gilpin] Fur returns measure what trappers brought in, which depends on prices, effort and weather as well as on the animals.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A **phase plot** shows two populations at once; a cycle is a closed loop.
Add self-limitation (crowding) to the prey and the loop spirals in: the cycle dies away.
Fur records are not counts; prices, effort and weather affect them too.

blocks.text: Volterra came to the problem through his family. Umberto D'Ancona, a young marine biologist engaged to his daughter Luisa, had been studying the fish markets of the northern Adriatic.[^volterra] During the First World War, fishing in the Adriatic almost stopped, with the boats laid up and the waters mined. When D'Ancona looked at what was landed, he found that the share of sharks, rays and other predatory fish in the catch had gone up during the war years and fallen back after. Why should less fishing favour the predators?

blocks.caption: Share of sharks, rays and skates in the fish landed at the port of Fiume (now Rijeka), as D'Ancona tabulated it. Fishing nearly stopped from 1915 to 1918.

options.title: Predatory fish, percent of the catch

blocks.text: In Volterra's model, the populations swing round a balance point, and their averages over a cycle are the balance point itself. Now add fishing that takes the same share of both kinds every year. The prey lose some of their number to the nets, but they also lose some of their predators. The predators lose to the nets and lose some of their food. Work it through and the predators come off worse: fishing lowers the predators' average and raises the prey's.

blocks.caption: Volterra's model with fishing that takes the same share of both kinds each year: the average numbers over a cycle.
blocks.task: Guess, then fish at 30 percent a year or more

blocks.text: Run it backwards and you have D'Ancona's war: stop fishing and the predators recover more than their prey, so their share of the catch goes up. The result is called **Volterra's principle**, and it has an awkward consequence. A poison or a harvest that kills predator and prey alike tends to help the prey.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: **Volterra's principle**: removing the same share of predators and prey raises the prey's average and lowers the predators'.
It explains why predatory fish made up more of the Adriatic catch when wartime fishing stopped.

blocks.text: Models and ledgers can only suggest. To find out what really drives the hare cycle, the Canadian ecologist Charles Krebs and his colleagues ran an experiment on a large scale. From 1986 to 1996, in the boreal forest around Kluane Lake in the Yukon, they fenced off square-kilometre blocks of forest with electric fences that kept out lynx and coyotes (though not owls and hawks). In other blocks they scattered extra food for the hares. In some they did both, and they left others alone for comparison. Then they followed the hares through a whole cycle.

blocks.caption: Hare numbers in the Kluane experiment during the decline, compared with blocks left alone (Krebs and colleagues, 1995).

options.title: Hares, times the number in blocks left alone

blocks.text: Neither treatment alone stopped the cycle. Fencing out predators doubled the hares; extra food tripled them; both together gave about eleven times as many, far more than either alone. Krebs's reading was that the cycle comes from predators and food working together, neither enough alone. Later work by his colleague Rudy Boonstra added another factor: hares chased by predators show signs of stress and breed less, so the threat of being eaten lowers births as well as raising deaths.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Krebs's fences and food at Kluane: fencing out predators doubled hares, food tripled them, both together gave about eleven times as many.
The hare cycle comes from predators and food acting together.

blocks.text: Volterra's principle turns up wherever people kill animals without picking and choosing. In the 1880s, Californian citrus groves were nearly destroyed by the cottony cushion scale, a sap-sucking insect from Australia. The fix was a predator from its homeland, the vedalia ladybird, which ate it down within a couple of years.[^vedalia] In the late 1940s growers started spraying their groves with the new insecticide DDT. The spray killed scale insects and ladybirds alike, and the scale bounced back first, just as Volterra's fish predicted. Outbreaks of the scale followed the spraying, until growers learned to spare the ladybirds.

Farmers now call this **pest resurgence**: a spray that kills a pest's enemies along with the pest can make the pest worse a season later. Predators usually breed more slowly than their prey, so they take longer to recover. It is the same arithmetic as the lynx, a year or two behind the hares.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Killing predator and prey alike tends to help the prey: spraying a pest can make it worse by killing its enemies.
Predators usually breed more slowly than their prey, so they recover later.

blocks.caption: Six questions on predators and prey
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: In Lotka and Volterra's model, which comes first: the peak in prey or the peak in predators?
choices: Prey first, predators a little after
items.why: Predators multiply on the prey they eat, so they keep rising while prey are plentiful and peak only once the prey are already falling.

items.ask: A lake's pike and perch cycle. A new law has anglers take 20 percent of each kind every year. In Volterra's model, what happens to the average number of perch (the prey)?
items.why: Taking the same share of both hits the predators twice, through the nets and through their food. Their average falls, and with fewer predators the prey's average goes up.

items.ask: On a phase plot of hares across and lynx up, a run spirals inward to a point. What does that mean?
choices: The cycle is dying away and both populations are settling to steady numbers
items.why: A closed loop is a cycle that repeats. A spiral inward means each swing is smaller than the last, settling on a balance point that is not zero.

items.ask: In Krebs's Kluane experiment, fencing out predators alone doubled the hares, and food alone tripled them. Both together gave about eleven times as many. What does that suggest?
choices: Food and predators work together, each making the other's effect stronger
Food is the only real cause
Predators are the only real cause
items.why: If the two effects simply added, both together would give about four or five times as many. Eleven times means each made the other stronger: well-fed hares with no predators could breed freely, which neither treatment allowed alone.

items.ask: A farmer sprays a field heavily for aphids every week. Ladybirds, which eat aphids, are killed too. What is the likely result a few weeks after the spraying stops?
choices: The aphids bounce back faster than the ladybirds, and may be worse than before
The ladybirds come back first and keep the aphids down
items.why: Predators usually breed more slowly than their prey, and the spray removed both. The aphids recover first: pest resurgence, Volterra's principle in a field.

items.ask: Why are fur returns not a perfect record of how many lynx there were?
choices: They depend on how hard trappers worked, fur prices and weather, not only on the lynx
The Company only bought hare pelts
items.why: A pelt record measures catch, which is effort times success. In a year of high prices trappers work harder; in a bad winter they catch less.

summary: **Hare and lynx numbers rise and fall about every ten years.** The Hudson's Bay Company's fur records show it, with lynx peaks a year or two after hares'.
**Two stocks that feed each other can cycle.** In Lotka and Volterra's model, prey feed predators and predators eat prey, so both swing, predators behind.
**A phase plot shows the cycle as a loop.** If the prey are also limited by their own crowding, the loop spirals in and the cycle dies away.
**Fishing both kinds favours the prey.** Volterra's principle: taking the same share of predator and prey lowers the predators' average and raises the prey's.
**It explained D'Ancona's fish.** When wartime fishing stopped in the Adriatic, predators made up more of the catch.
**At Kluane, food and predators worked together.** Fencing out predators doubled the hares, food tripled them, both gave about eleven times as many.
**Spraying a pest can make it worse.** Killing its predators too leads to pest resurgence.

gilpin.title: Do hares eat lynx?
gilpin.text: That was the title of Michael Gilpin's 1973 paper. Plotted as a loop, the Company's hare and lynx numbers from some decades turn clockwise, which in a predator-prey model would mean the prey were eating the predators. Gilpin didn't believe it, of course. He suggested the records were shaped by things the model leaves out, such as trapping effort, disease among the hares, and the fact that hare numbers were partly reconstructed from reports rather than pelts. The joke made a serious point about reading models into data.

elton.title: Elton and the Hudson's Bay Company
elton.text: The Canadian naturalist C. Gordon Hewitt had plotted the Company's fur returns in his 1921 book *The Conservation of the Wild Life of Canada*. Elton read Hewitt, then persuaded the Hudson's Bay Company to hire him as a consultant in 1925 and let him into its London archives. At first Elton guessed the ten-year cycle might be driven by sunspots, which follow an eleven-year rhythm, before the evidence turned him against the idea.

volterra.title: Vito Volterra
volterra.text: Volterra (1860–1940) was already one of Italy's leading mathematicians and a senator of the kingdom when D'Ancona brought him the fish tables in 1925. In 1931 he was one of only twelve Italian university professors, out of more than twelve hundred, who refused to swear an oath of loyalty to Mussolini's fascist regime, and he lost his chair in Rome.

vedalia.title: The vedalia beetle
vedalia.text: In 1888 the entomologist Albert Koebele travelled to Australia to find what kept the cottony cushion scale scarce in its native home. He shipped back a few hundred vedalia ladybirds (*Rodolia cardinalis*) packed on ice. Bred in mesh tents over infested orange trees in Los Angeles, the beetles cleared whole orchards within months and saved the Californian citrus industry for a total travel bill of about $1,500.
